newsitem.title: UK: Dollar bid in Europe as data sour German outlook.
newsitem.headline: Dollar bid in Europe as data sour German outlook.

text.p: The dollar was raring to go at European midsession after hitting five-week highs as a German jobless increase stoked doubts on monetary union and contrasted vividly with an expected jump in U.S. non-farm payrolls.

German unemployment rose a seasonally-adjusted 56,000 in May to a total of 4.358 million, a rate of 11.4 percent. The Federal Labour Office said Bonn's forecast of 3.95 million average 1997 unemployment now looked out of reach.
The figures intensified concerns over how Germany would cut its budget deficit to 3.0 percent of GDP to qualify for the European single currency.

"The German jobless numbers are making people ask what Kohl and Waigel are going to do about their budget problems and make them more inclined to hold long dollar positions," said Chris Tinker, chief treasury economist at Standard Chartered.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and embattled finance minister Theo Waigel have repeatedly declared their commitment to meeting EMU criteria strictly and on time, despite Germany's sizeable budget shortfall.
The dollar stood at 1.7354/64 marks at 1040 GMT, up from late Thursday's 1.7292/97. Earlier it hit 1.7373, its strongest level since reaching a 1997 high of 1.7389 on April 28.
"The market still really likes the dollar and can think of nothing better to buy," said Nick Probert, head of spot trading at Bank of America here.

A bullish dollar/Swiss -- which has gained four francs since the beginning of the week -- helped propel dollar/mark upwards, dealers said. The U.S. unit stood at 1.4580/90 francs at 1046 GMT versus late yesterday's European level of 1.4479/88.

With the rise in German unemployment already weighing on dollar/mark, the German unit was expected to take a further hit when U.S. May payrolls data appeared at 1230 GMT. Consensus expectations are for a 219,000 increase in payrolls.
A strong number is seen boosting the dollar as it feeds speculation that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its next policy-making meeting on July 1/2.

Sterling was propelled higher after the Bank of England hiked official interest rates by a quarter-point to 6.5 percent. The tightening followed the first meeting of the BoE's monetary policy committee, formed after the new Labour government handed responsibility for setting rates to the central bank.
The pound spiked up over half a pfennig to around 2.8270 marks after the rate rise, before pulling back to 2.8230/40 by 1118 GMT. It ended in Europe at 2.8210/20 on Thursday.

The current deep uncertainty over European monetary union was yet another millstone around the mark's neck. European Union finance ministers meet on Sunday and Monday to discuss EMU at what the market fears will be a stormy gathering.

The German-inspired stability pact -- aimed at enforcing budgetary rigour after the euro is launched in 1999 -- is expected to top the agenda, amid concerns France's new left-wing government will attempt to reopen discussion of the agreement.
A Dutch EU presidency spokesman said, however, that France had not officially requested any reopening of the pact.

Analysts expressed fears that the EU meeting could stir talk of EMU delay. While that is normally seen as mark-positive, the uncertainty it would create is likely to boost the mark as players seek safe havens away from EMU turmoil, they said.

"The risks are for further political uncertainty in Europe and the economic activity data pointing more towards the U.S. dollar gaining ground rather than being reversed," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Banque Paribas.
Dollar/yen was sidelined and stuck, trading at 115.75/81 at 1143 GMT versus late Thursday's 115.63/68.
